question: Linda is 31, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy, is deeply concerned with discrimination and social justice, and took part in anti-nuclear demonstrations. Is it more probable that Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement than that Linda is a bank teller?

claims.text: The description of Linda fits the feminist movement well.
By resemblance to a stereotype, 'bank teller and feminist' can look like a better fit than 'bank teller' alone.
Many people answer yes because of the representativeness heuristic.
The question asks about probability, which is subject to strict logical constraints.
Every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller, so feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers.
P(bank teller and feminist) is less than or equal to P(bank teller).
The conjunction rule holds regardless of the description given.
Adding detail can make a story more vivid or typical but never makes a conjunction more probable than one of its parts.
Resemblance to the description may make the conjunction feel more plausible but cannot override the conjunction rule.
